name: Ursa Major
description: Containing several nearby stars, Ursa Major is distorted, but still recognizable. ξ Ursae Majoris is pushed out of the constellation, and Pollux (seen in Gemini from Earth) makes an appearance.

name: Pisces
description: The "circlet" of piscis austrinis is unrecognizable, with γ Piscium drifting to the other side of β Piscium, and ι Piscium being shifted outside the constellation entirely. The rest of the constellation is fairly intact.

name: Cetus
description: The shape of Cetus is largely intact, with a couple nearby stars (including μ Ceti and τ Ceti) shifted out of the constellation.

name: Pegasus
description: Alpheratz (technically in Andromeda, at least by Earth's definition) is shifted quite severely, as to make the famous "square of Pegasus" no longer resemble a square. θ Pegasi is similarly nearby, but overall the constellation is not distorted too badly.

name: Hercules
description: ζ Herculis is close enough that its apparent drift throws off most interpretations of this constellation. Nearby stars shifted into here include Vega and Sol.

name: Leo
description: Leo contains several nearby stars and its shape is unrecognizable.

name: Virgo
description: Though the sideways stick figure is still visible, some of the individual stars (particularly β Virginis) have shifted significantly, and Sirius makes a conspicuous appearance that draws attention away from Virgo itself.

name: Centaurus and Crux
description: Centaurus contains several stars close to Sol, most famously α Centauri, which is now nowhere to be seen. Some parts of the centaur are relatively okay, some are distorted quite badly, and some are missing entirely. Crux fares even worse, with γ Crucis being shifted into the centaur's lower torso.

name: Draco and Ursa Minor
description: Ursa Minor fares worse than its larger sibling. The familiar shape of the "dipper" is nowhere to be seen, and the constellation is not circumpolar. Draco's meandering body is the same shape, but its head is more triangular, as ν Draconis is relatively close to Sol.

name: Boötes and Canes Venatici
description: Boötes is nearly on the opposite side of Sol from Erid, so even the nearby stars stay in the constellation — though its shape is distorted. α Canum Venaticorum is a naked-eye double.

name: Taurus
description: The main shape of Taurus is difficult to recognize, though β Tauri is replaced by π<sup>3</sup> Orionis. Taurus contains two significant star clusters, the Hyades and the Pleiades.

name: Orion
description: Orion consists mostly of distant stars, so its shape is completely intact (here shown upside-down, since Erid's north-south axis is roughly antiparallel Earth's). Only χ<sup>1</sup> Orionis and π<sup>3</sup> Orionis are close enough to be shifted out of the constellation.

name: Sagittarius
description: Both the "teapot" and Terebellum are unrecognizable. Two pairs of stars which are clearly distinct from Earth (σ Sagittarii and τ Sagittarii; ζ Sagittarii and φ Sagittarii) form visual doubles.

name: Camelopardalis
description: The faint constellation of Camelopardalis is Erid's southernmost constellation.

name: Cepheus
description: Though Cepheus contains some distant stars, α Cephei and γ Cephei are close enough that the pentagon is unrecognizable. β Cassiopeiae is shifted into this constellation and outshines all the stars we know of as Cepheus.

name: Cassiopeia
description: Though half of the famous "W" of Cassiopeia is intact, ε Cassiopeiae is in a significantly different spot, and β Cassiopeiae is shifted out of the constellation entirely.

name: Octans and Chamaeleon
description: Octans and Chamaeleon contain no bright stars, so this region of sky appears nearly empty — though α Trianguli Australis is on the border of this region. Erid has no easily visible north pole star.

name: Canis Major
description: Though most of the individual stars of Canis Major are distant, its brightest star, Sirius, is rather close to Sol. You could still draw a dog with the visible stars, in a different orientation from Earth's.
